articles.title: In 2017, a Florida woman had a daughter under a sperm donor agreement, and a man later named the child in his will; after his death, an October 21 court upheld denial of the child's claim to his Florida home
articles.summary: A Florida appeals court on Wednesday,upheld an earlier decision denying a young girl's claim to a house owned by a deceased man who had named her in his
articles.body: A Florida appeals court on Wednesday,upheld an earlier decision denying a young girl's claim to a house owned by a deceased man who had named her in his will. The case involved Melissa Azrack, who gave birth to the girl in 2017, and Malcolm Dorman, who died in March 2021. Although Dorman had described himself as the child's biological father, an earlier sperm donor agreement and a dispute over the legal status of his house complicated the claim. The appeal ultimately failed because Azrack had not challenged a separate finding about the property.According to the judgment available on Justia, Azrack and Dorman had entered into a sperm donor agreement before the girl's birth. The agreement stated that Azrack would be the child's only intended legal parent and that Dorman would give up any parental rights he might have.However, Dorman later described himself as the girl's biological father, including in his will. He also left certain benefits for her and named her as a beneficiary of a trust, an arrangement through which assets can be held for another person's benefit. After his death, Azrack claimed that he had intended one of his houses in Golden Beach, Florida, to benefit her daughter.What followed was a dispute over the child's relationship with Dorman and whether she could claim the house. The earlier court rejected the claim for two reasons. It found that the girl had not been established as Dorman's legal or biological daughter. It also concluded that the house did not qualify for the particular legal protection under which she was claiming it. The second finding eventually became the main reason her appeal failed.How the dispute over the house beganDorman owned several properties when he died in March 2021. John McDonald was appointed to manage his estate, including the properties and other assets he left behind.Azrack later approached the court on behalf of her daughter, identified in court documents as E.M.A. She wanted the court to determine the status of Dorman's house at 443 Ocean Boulevard in Golden Beach.She argued that Dorman had intended the property to pass into a trust for the girl's benefit. However, McDonald, representing Dorman's estate, opposed the claim.The estate questioned whether the child could legally be treated as Dorman's daughter. It pointed to the sperm donor agreement, under which Azrack was the only intended legal parent. The estate also maintained that Dorman was not the girl's biological father.The trial court examined the agreement and the evidence concerning the child's parentage. It found that Dorman had given up his legal parental rights under the agreement. The court also concluded that Azrack had not presented enough evidence to establish that he was the girl's biological father or had otherwise legally acknowledged her as his child.But there was another problem with the claim. The court found that the Golden Beach house was not Dorman's protected homestead. Under Florida law, this refers to a property that qualifies for certain protections concerning a person's home.This meant that even if the girl had been recognised as Dorman's daughter, she would still not have succeeded in claiming the house on that basis.Why the mother lost her appealAzrack disagreed with the earlier court's findings about her daughter's relationship with Dorman. She challenged those findings and questioned how the court had considered the evidence.However, she did not challenge the separate decision concerning the house itself. That made a difference when the case reached Florida's Third District Court of Appeal.The judges explained that the earlier ruling had been based on two separate reasons. Even if one reason was successfully challenged, the decision would remain in place because the other reason had not been disputed.In Azrack's case, the finding that the Golden Beach house was not protected homestead property remained unchanged. Therefore, reconsidering whether Dorman was the girl's father would not have altered the outcome of the property dispute.The appeals court consequently upheld the rejection of the claim. Importantly, it did not independently decide whether Dorman was the child's biological father.The case continued after the first rulingThe dispute had also led to further proceedings after the original decision.Azrack sought the removal of the judge who had heard the case, and her request was granted in May 2024. After another judge took over, she asked the court to cancel the earlier judgment or reconsider some of its findings. Both requests were rejected.Azrack then challenged those decisions before the appeals court. However, the judges found that the requests had not been made under procedures permitted for this type of case, which concerned the estate of a deceased person. As a result, that part of her appeal was dismissed.Another disagreement concerned whether the earlier judgment could apply to Azrack personally, rather than only to her role as her daughter's representative.The appeals court found no error in this aspect of the ruling, noting that Azrack had also taken part in the case in her personal capacity.The earlier court had also found that Dorman's estate was entitled to recover legal fees and costs. However, the appeals court said it was too early to consider whether Azrack could personally be required to pay them because no amount had yet been decided.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two killed in attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
articles.summary: It is the latest in a series of attacks by the Houthi movement which have targeted airports and other sites in the kingdom.
articles.body:
Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says.

Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals.

The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles.

On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said.

The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze.

It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.

Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.

US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate

UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged

At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.

One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The Houthis' military spokesman said on Wednesday that they had targeted military equipment at an airport in the southern Yemeni city of al-Mukalla, which it said had been transported by Saudi Arabia for use by pro-government forces.

Meanwhile, Houthi-run media reported that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.

According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.

The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.

The UN says more than 256,000 people have also been displaced.

The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.

Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support.

However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces.

articles.title: ‘Facebook’s wrongdoing’: Why has Meta been fined $25bn in New Mexico?
articles.summary: The tech giant has been accused of misleading users regarding data privacy linked to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
articles.body:
A judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta Platforms to pay the US state $25bn after a court found the company intentionally misled consumers about the privacy of their data.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to ⁠the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.

The judge found that a penalty of more than $219bn was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25bn.

New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against ⁠a company in United States history.

CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company was confident it would win on appeal.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech ‌to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”

New Mexico’s attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

Cambridge Analytica, a now-defunct British political consulting firm, harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political advertisements during the 2016 election season, when it worked for Donald Trump’s successful presidential campaign.

The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data and its handling of hate speech ⁠and misinformation posted on the platform.

Lawyers for the state cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed in which Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the company did not sell user data.

They alleged the company knew third parties had broad access to users’ data and tolerated hate speech ⁠or other harmful content when it benefitted the company’s bottom line.

Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, said the judgement “should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley”.

Meta is facing thousands of lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers over the impact of Instagram and Facebook on teen mental health.

A trial brought by a coalition of state attorneys general in a California federal court began in August over claims the company engineered Facebook and Instagram to be addictive to children, which could expose the company to huge damages and force it to make sweeping changes to its platforms.

It will also address claims by 29 states that the company illegally collected and used children’s data in violation of federal law.

Six other states settled their lawsuits related to Cambridge Analytica for $459m, as part of a $17bn multistate ‌settlement Meta reached in August to resolve states’ claims that the company’s platforms had harmed teen mental health.

Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942m in two trials against Meta over claims it ⁠facilitated sexual exploitation of young people on Instagram and Facebook and misled consumers about the platforms’ safety.

The American Economic Liberties Project, a nonprofit that supports stronger policies towards corporations, said the latest fine of $25bn is “a drop in the bucket for Meta”, but demonstrates that people want accountability.

“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” the nonprofit’s Executive Director Nidhi Hegde said. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”

articles.title: Rubio, Hegseth point fingers at Musk in Starlink slowdown
articles.summary: Top Trump administration officials are starting to point fingers squarely at SpaceX founder Elon Musk for the decision to slow down his company’s Starlink satellite internet services and its military counterpart Starshield for Ukraine, which has been muddled in uncertainty over the culprit. Looking to deflect the controversial move — which was swiftly admonished by…
articles.body:
Top Trump administration officials are starting to point fingers squarely at SpaceX founder Elon Musk for the decision to slow down his company’s Starlink satellite internet services and its military counterpart Starshield for Ukraine, which has been muddled in uncertainty over the culprit.

Looking to deflect the controversial move — which was swiftly admonished by powerful Congressional Republicans and Democrats — Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink was up to Musk and not the White House.

“The bottom ​line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio told reporters while traveling to India.

And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking to reporters ​a day prior on Tuesday, suggested Starlink’s slowdown was a commercial matter and not a result of any orders from the White House.

“There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” Hegseth said.

Taken together, the comments are a change of tune to President Trump’s original assertions last week that neither he nor Musk were responsible for the disruption. Rubio also on Saturday had insisted that no one ordered the slowdown.

The about-face comes after The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown of the satellite services, a vital tool Ukraine uses to defend itself from Russian missile and drone attacks.

Trump’s role is unclear. The Journal reported that at least one person claimed Musk and Trump spoke prior to the slowdown. Reuters reported last week that the order to throttle Starlink came from inside the White House, in a directive to the Pentagon. Sources speaking to Reuters did not specify who at the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order.

“I don’t know who did it but I was not involved,” Trump told reporters Wednesday when asked.

Trump and Musk have experienced periods of fall-out in their relationship but appear on the upswing today. The nadir of their relationship occurred during a major public spat in June 2025, where Musk alleged that files on the disgraced financier and convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein were kept secret to protect Trump.

But the relationship has rebounded since then. Trump awarded Musk the National Medal of Science earlier this month. And Musk has provided more than $276 million for Republicans in the midterm elections, the New York Times reported .

Outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) on Wednesday said he doubted Trump had no hand in the slowdown, as he doesn’t believe that Musk “would do this without at least the acquiescence of the White House.”

“I think it’s frankly shameful,” Cornyn said on CNBC’s Squawk Box. “I think we should be supporting the victim, not the aggressor.”

Starlink’s slowdown in Ukraine came after Ukrainian President Voldoymyr Zelensky lashed out at Trump for waiving sanctions on Russia and making a deal to purchase diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin. Zelensky called Trump “weak” for making the deal.

Part of Trump’s response to Zelensky was to blame him as the obstacle to peace with Putin.

Republicans holding back blame on Trump for Starlink’s throttling are demanding an investigation and accountability. Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) and outgoing congressman Don Bacon (R-Neb.) have threatened to block Trump’s agenda during the lame-duck session if answers are not provided.

“This is a very, very serious matter. It cannot be glossed over,” Fitzpatrick told CNN on Tuesday, following the Journal report.

Fitzpatrick said if Musk ordered Starshield’s slowdown, “that is likely a violation of the law.”

“He has decision-making authority over Starlink, the civilian commercial product, but not Starshield, which is a military grade national security tool. No individual civilian should have any decision-making authority over how that’s deployed,” he said.

Adding to the confusion, Rubio, who also serves as national security advisor, has said Ukraine does not have access to Starshield.

“Starshield is a defense product… the United States military uses,” Rubio told reporters last week.

“It’s not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that’s under conversation. It’s under discussion right now of how they would want to use it.”

Zelensky on Tuesday said he discussed with Rubio “the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored,” and called the conversation “constructive,” in a post on the social platform X .

Part of that conversation is whether the U.S. could give Ukraine the ability to hit targets deep inside Russia, in particular missile launchers, in exchange for halting Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries.

Trump has demanded Ukraine halt strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that they are related to high diesel prices in the U.S. that largely stem from the U.S. war against Iran.

Russia has refused to halt strikes against Ukrainian energy sites, in particular civilian electricity and heating infrastructure. Zelensky’s allies in Congress have backed a proposal for the U.S. to give Ukraine the ability to hit Russian missile launchers in exchange for halting Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy facilities.

“President Trump can lower prices at the pump today by simply agreeing to this deal!” Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) wrote in a post on X Sunday. Wicker’s pushback came after Trump announced he would buy Russian diesel to lower prices in the U.S.

Ukraine’s ability to hit Russian launchers would rely on accessing Starlink inside Russia, where it’s currently blocked. A bipartisan group of lawmakers — seven Republicans and 16 Democrats — wrote to Trump on Wednesday urging him to call Musk and give Ukrainians that access.

“With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate,” the lawmakers wrote.

“If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian ‘arrows,’ it must be able to shoot the ‘archer.’ The Starlink system run by Mr. Musk’s company SpaceX could help with that.”

articles.title: After a Black media empire fell, a photographer explored the extraordinary building it left behind
articles.summary: The Johnson Publishing Company commissioned a historic high rise in Chicago in 1972 that became a monument to Black culture. Four decades later, the photographer Barbara Karant explored the empty building it left behind.
articles.body: Just four years after the Civil Rights era, Chicago welcomed its first downtown high rise designed by a Black architect for a Black-owned company. For four decades, the Johnson Publishing Company occupied an 11-story tower at 820 S. Michigan Avenue that was a monument to Black culture, sending out millions of copies of Ebony and Jet magazines each year. The company’s founder, publisher John H. Johnson, called it “the miracle on Michigan Avenue” for having been built at all. The media titan elevated the stories, news and beauty of Black life, and attracted unrivaled cover stars including Grace Jones, Prince, Donna Summer, Michael Jordan, Florence Griffith Joyner and President Barack Obama. But as the company struggled in the 2010s, it sold off its iconic titles to a venture capitalist firm, and major art world institutions and artists acquired its archives, art collection and furnishings in the hopes of preserving its legacy. The physical building, though emptied out, remained. Housed inside the austere modernist facade by architect John Moutoussamy, the interiors — the work of Palm Springs designers Arthur Elrod and William Raiser — were never renovated or changed. They had painted the walls in colorful chevrons, peacock feathers, and swirling hues of orange, green and purple, and carpeted the floors with equally exuberant patterns. The office was vacated by 2012, less than a decade after Johnson’s death, and from there the company eventually declared bankruptcy. Inside its former headquarters, which had housed Ebony, Jet and Fashion Fair cosmetics and a cafeteria so popular that stars and public figures often asked for the menu in advance, the guest list quickly dwindled to one: a photographer who, as she put it, became “obsessed” with the empty building and its history and set out to preserve it. Now, Barbara Karant’s collected images are part of a new book on the Johnson Publishing Company’s legacy, called “820 Ebony/Jet: Visions of the Johnson Publishing Company, an American Icon.” Through her photographs, archival images, and guest essays on the building’s history, the book reflects on the company as “the heart and soul of Black America,” and shows the tangible loss of a cultural powerhouse. “I was completely enamored of the environment and the vitality,” Karant explained. “I really felt, despite the fact that the building was empty, that there was a real residual creativity and energy that remained.” Karant, an architecture and interiors photographer who is based in Chicago, spoke about the project over video along with Joy Bennett, a former senior editor at Ebony. The two experienced the building in entirely different ways. Bennett, the daughter of Ebony executive editor Lerone Bennett Jr. and Jet editor Gloria Bennett, quite literally grew up with the building, first as her parents’ place of work and then as her own from the late ’90s until 2009. Karant only visited the space after it had been sold to Columbia College Chicago, where she taught as an adjunct professor. She visited it some 40 times beginning in 2013, usually in the spring and fall, because it lacked AC during sweltering summers and was only heated enough to keep the pipes from bursting in the winter, she recalled. Since completing her project, the building, whose exteriors were landmarked, has been redeveloped into residential units, with the only hint of its past the remaining rooftop sign. (Ebony and Jet magazines changed hands multiple times and are still published digitally under the ownership of Eden Bridgeman Sklenar, who currently serves as its CEO). When it was built, Bennett said, “It was a testament to Mr. Johnson’s faith, and hope, and success. It was a vibrant workspace, unbelievable. I can’t even explain how important it was to Black America.” Prior to that, the Johnsons ran their business out of a former funeral home that required a white intermediary to purchase it. When Johnson decided he wanted a new headquarters, he grew frustrated with trying to find investors and funded the project himself. On any given day, Bennett recalled, the staff could encounter Hollywood stars like Jamie Foxx or Elizabeth Taylor, the Reverend Jesse Jackson or the sex therapist Dr. Ruth; her mother would recall stories of Louis Armstrong or Lena Horne walking the same halls. In the book, others share their encounters: Lionel Richie taking the elevator up, or Sidney Poitier signing autographs, or Michael Jackson arriving incognito. After senator Obama became President-elect Obama in 2008, he sat down with Ebony for his first print interview following the historic election. “The Secret Service locked us down. We couldn’t leave the floor,” Bennett recalled. “It was crazy.” But before pursuing her journalism career, Bennett gave tours of the building. There was the bustling cafeteria, Fashion Fair’s dressing rooms, the Ebony Test Kitchen, and artworks by Jacob Lawrence and Richard Hunt, not to mention the barbershop, fitness room, and apartment on the executive floor. Upstairs, the bold reds and sharp angles of Johnson’s suite contrasted with the cream and honey softness of his wife Eunice’s office. It was an extension of Johnson himself, and when he died, his casket was laid out in the foyer of the building, Bennett said, with a line down Michigan Avenue to pay respects. When Bennett cut her teeth at other media companies including Gannett and Crain’s before her homecoming back to the Johnson Publishing Company, she said every other office space she had encountered, by comparison, was “dull and drab.” “You mean everybody doesn’t have these colorful floors, these textures, the glass and mirrors, and artists and sculptors who do the design?” she remembered thinking. Karant experienced the same wonder of the space, even once it had been hollowed out. When she photographed the 110,000 square feet of space, she was always alone, and no matter how many times she visited, whenever she returned she’d find something new. As she was making the book and spoke to former employees, she was often asked which floor was her favorite. “I guess everybody had different favorite floors,” she said. “But my favorite floor was always the floor I was working on.” Though it’s no longer possible to experience the building the way it was, it can be visited in different ways — through Karant’s book, or the artworks of Lorna Simspson or Theaster Gates, who both turn to the archives of Jet and Ebony in their personal practices. Gates, who now stewards the photographic archives and periodicals of the Johnson Publishing Company, has exhibited it in different forms. Earlier this year, he mounted a permanent public artwork incorporating some of the images of Black life and beauty at the Obama Presidential Center. Through her own project, Karant has joined a group of artists determined to give the Johnson Publishing Company a second life. “Architecture, interiors, environments tell stories about the people that were there and the people that may be there in the future,” she said. “As far as this project, I felt that it just warranted the attention and the care to document it. People need to know about it.”

Former Ebony staff photographer Isaac Sutton with the model Charmayne Caldwell in JPC's in-house photo studio in1972.
The design from 1972, when the building opened, remained in tact with original carpeting, wallpaper, and appliances.
The JPC library on the 7th floor featured thousands of books on Black American and African history and culture.
Karant could only work in the more temperate months since there was no air conditioning and little heat.
The photographer became obsessed with all the little details of the building, and the echoes of its past.
The vibrant interiors were the work of Palm Springs designers Arthur Elrod and William Raiser.

The building remained empty while it was owned by Columbia College Chicago, where Karant worked as an adjunct professor, but it has since been developed into residential units, with only the exteriors preserved.
The retro designs, which differed from room to room, and floor to floor, provided endless color and texture to document.

articles.title: Macron has one more chance to save the country or ‘it’s lost for France,’ business owner warns
articles.summary: A French business owner who had five family stores destroyed by looters warns of growing insecurity and urges authorities to protect businesses ahead of another weekend of protests.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A French business owner who had five of her family's stores wrecked by looters last week said this coming Saturday's protest could be a watershed moment for France. Her message to President Emmanuel Macron: "Next Saturday is your last chance to save France," Michele Teboul, the business owner, said in an interview with Fox News Digital. Addressing both Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and Macron, she said, "If they don't do whatâs necessary to do next Saturday, I think it is lost for France." Teboul lost more than merchandise when looters ransacked 15 of the stores owned by her family, leaving five completely destroyed. She also lost faith in her governmentâs ability to protect them. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: FRANCE BRACES FOR MORE UNREST AFTER PARTS OF PARIS SPUN OUT OF CONTROL Teboul accused authorities of failing to provide enough police to protect businesses, leaving families like hers facing destroyed stores and a costly recovery. She demanded that they protect the population before another Saturday. Her retail operations include stores in Paris, Bordeaux, Lyon, Marseille and Montpellier. Her sons work within the same company and operate their own brand, she said. For her family, protections put in place before the violence proved insufficient. Attackers used axes to break through boarding, she said, leaving her sons facing a difficult recovery. "We can say that five of the most important stores have been looted," she said, describing those locations as "completely destroyed." Now, her family needs to pay for additional protection while trying to meet insurance security requirements. Teboul said it would take at least two months to repair and secure the stores to the required standards. She described those requirements as a condition for obtaining insurance coverage, adding another obstacle to reopening and recovering the business. "I think the winter season is dead," she said. VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED Companies with established operations and financial reserves may be able to absorb the disruption, she said. Younger businesses face a more difficult path. "The government said they would help us," Teboul said. "We are going to see." Her sons have hired security guards with dogs. She also said she had heard of other shopkeepers obtaining weapons or tear gas, emphasizing that her sons had not purchased weapons. "Some have bought weapons," she said. "You know, we are not used to weapons in France." The concern extends beyond damaged merchandise and storefronts. Teboul, who is Jewish, said that many Jews are considering leaving France and warned that further disorder could deepen that uncertainty if things don't get better. SOME SYNAGOGUES CANCELED PRAYERS AS FRENCH JEWS FACED WARNINGS AMID VIOLENT PROTESTS "It is going to be very hard to imagine a future in France for us, especially for Jews," she said of her hope that the coming Saturday would be different. Teboul said Jewish schools, synagogues and community businesses have dedicated security arrangements. Teboul is a former director of CRIF is the umbrella organization representing French Jewish institutions. She stressed, however, that the weekend's violence was a national problem affecting people beyond the Jewish community. "The specific problem of last Saturday is not a problem of Jews," she said. "The whole of France is concerned by this problem." Teboul said looters sought street-wear and expensive merchandise. She accused police of failing to protect businesses during the unrest on Saturday, saying officers were overwhelmed as large crowds descended on city centers, particularly in Marseille and Lyon. She cited an estimate she had heard being talked of as being around 30,000 young people arriving in central Marseille, a figure Fox News Digital could not independently verify. French October 17: Leading French broadcaster BFM reported on its X account that "Between 1,800 and 3,000 people" engaged in "the ransacking of the city center of Marseille, according to the prosecutor's estimates." MACRON JETS OUT OF RIOT-TORN FRANCE FOR GULF TRIP AS POLITICAL PRESSURE MOUNTS "They were not enough," she said of the police. The French government has acknowledged failures in its response to the unrest. She said that authorities had mistaken the threat for an ordinary demonstration. "Of course they could prevent it," she added. Teboul distinguished between students protesting over grievances and those who used the demonstrations as cover to steal. "There were two events on Saturday," she said. "The looters, they took the opportunity that there were many people downtown, and then they came." "We have to feel secure," she said. "We do not feel secure for the moment." Teboul warned that another failure to protect the population could also have consequences for the government of Emmanuel Macron. "The government may fall down," she said. articles.title: Hail the size of golf balls pummels parts of Arizona as rare storm moves through the West
articles.summary: PHOENIX — Hail the size of golf balls and damaging wind gusts pounded northern and central Arizona in a rare storm blowing through, bringing with it tornado risks and possible flash floods.
articles.body: PHOENIX — Hail the size of golf balls and damaging wind gusts pounded northern and central Arizona in a rare storm blowing through, bringing with it tornado risks and possible flash floods. The National Weather Service issued multiple warnings as severe thunderstorms moved through the state overnight Tuesday and into Wednesday, encouraging people to seek shelter and stay away from windows as damaging 2- to 3-inch) hail struck the area. Hail pummeled roofs, shattered windows and dented cars. Tornado watches were issued for multiple areas — the first the state has seen since October 2010. Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming off the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a weather service meteorologist in Flagstaff. “This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said. Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, with some landing on walls and carports. A few dozen ponderosa pines over 30 feet tall fell down in the Coconino National Forest, northwest of Flagstaff. “These are not small trees that are down," Bernhart said. “These are pretty strong trees that had been knocked down.” The greatest threat to the Phoenix metro area is heavy rainfall and flash flooding tonight and Thursday morning, said Mark O’Malley, a meteorologist at the weather service office in Phoenix.

articles.title: Storm Adam flooding: At least four dead in southern France
articles.summary: The deaths include two women found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.
articles.body:
At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.

The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.

The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.

Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead . Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.

In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.

Roads and train lines ‌in ⁠the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post ​on X.

"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."

More severe weather is forecast in France, with Storm Austen - a newly named weather system moving in from the Atlantic - expected to reach the country's north-west.

France's weather service, Météo-France, has issued an orange-level wind warning for five western departments from Thursday evening into Friday.

The alert covers Côtes-d'Armor, Finistère, Morbihan, Ille-et-Vilaine and Manche.

Storm Adam had already brought severe flooding to eastern Spain, where at least three people were killed.

Several towns along the Mediterranean coast were cut off by floodwaters, while helicopters were deployed to rescue people stranded on rooftops.

Members of the Military Emergencies Unit found the body of a woman in the town of Oliva, Valencia, during rescue operations on Monday.

Two other women were confirmed dead over ⁠the weekend. One woman's body was washed up on a beach in Sagunto, in the eastern region of Valencia, and another was swept away by floodwaters in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a promise that the national government would provide resources to help in reconstruction during a visit to the Valencia region on Tuesday.

The Valencian government approved on Tuesday an aid package of €23.5m (£20m) for those affected by Storm Adam.

articles.title: TOI Bharat Abroad: Vance face heat over H-1B rhetoric & Canada's points game
articles.summary: An Indian-origin voter has pushed JD Vance to reconsider his words on H-1B workers.
articles.body: An Indian-origin voter has pushed JD Vance to reconsider his words on H-1B workers. Canada is reopening a route that could help skilled Indian professionals secure permanent residency, while Telugu communities are taking Bathukamma celebrations across borders, blending tradition with science.So without further ado, let’s go.THE BIG STORYH-1B heat: Indian-origin voter challenges JD VanceJD Vance has acknowledged that his rhetoric about H-1B visa workers was imperfect, following a pointed exchange with an Indian-origin woman who had voted for him. The episode has brought fresh attention to the debate over skilled immigration in the United States, where Indian professionals remain among the biggest beneficiaries of the H-1B programme.The big pictureAt a CBS News town hall, Nivriti Agaram, a graduate of George Washington University, questioned Vance about his description of H-1B workers as “indentured servants”. She explained that she had voted for the Trump-Vance ticket after becoming a US citizen because of its positions on border security, drugs and trafficking, not because she believed immigrants were taking jobs away from Americans.Her intervention put the vice-president in an awkward position. Vance subsequently said his rhetoric had been imperfect and clarified that his criticism was directed at companies he believes exploit the visa system, rather than at foreign workers themselves.The exchange comes amid a wider immigration crackdown. The US administration has suspended eight technology companies, including Microsoft, Infosys and TCS, from filing new applications under the Permanent Labour Certification programme, a key step in many employer-sponsored green-card cases.Why it mattersIndians account for a substantial share of H-1B beneficiaries, making the debate particularly consequential for the community. The visa allows US employers to hire foreign professionals in specialised occupations, including technology, engineering and research.The argument is not simply about immigration numbers. It also concerns how the US balances domestic employment, access to global talent and the role foreign professionals play in its technology industry.Agaram's intervention is notable because she challenged Vance while identifying as someone who had supported his ticket. It also highlighted a distinction often lost in the political debate: criticism of employers' hiring practices is not necessarily the same as criticism of the workers they recruit.For Indian professionals, however, softer rhetoric does not remove the uncertainty created by policy changes. Visa rules, employer sponsorship and the route to permanent residency remain important concerns for people planning long-term careers in America.Read full storyNRI WATCHCanada's points game: Skilled Indian workers could gain an edgeCanada is adjusting its Express Entry immigration system in ways that could benefit skilled Indian professionals, particularly those with Canadian work experience in high-wage occupations.Under the changes announced by the Canadian government, qualifying candidates can receive additional points for eligible Canadian work experience in high-wage occupations. The revised system is scheduled to take effect on November 3, 2026.Eligible applicants could receive up to 70 additional points for qualifying experience, on top of their standard experience score. The changes also provide points for qualifying job offers in high-wage occupations, although candidates cannot claim both benefits at the same time under the stated rules.The high-wage category is determined by the occupation's median wage benchmark, rather than simply by how much an individual earns. To qualify, an occupation's median wage must be at least 1.3 times the median wage of the overall Canadian workforce.For Indian professionals, the change could make Canadian work experience more valuable when competing for permanent residency. It may be particularly relevant to people already working in Canada who want to turn temporary employment into a longer-term future.However, the changes do not guarantee permanent residency. Candidates still need to meet the relevant eligibility requirements and compete within the Express Entry system.Read full storyOFFBEATBathukamma blooms beyond bordersA festival rooted in Telangana's cultural traditions is finding new audiences overseas, as Telugu communities bring Bathukamma celebrations to countries including New Zealand and Malaysia.The festival centres on elaborate floral arrangements, songs and community gatherings. But overseas organisers are also finding new ways to make the tradition relevant to younger generations growing up far from India.In New Zealand, the Telugu Association organised a STEM-themed Bathukamma event on October 10, combining traditional floral displays with activities related to science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Children were introduced to scientific concepts through hands-on demonstrations alongside the festival's familiar flowers and cultural activities.Elsewhere, Telugu communities in Malaysia and Dubai have also been marking the occasion, creating spaces for people to connect with their language, traditions and shared heritage.Such celebrations offer more than a cultural gathering. For children raised abroad, they can provide an accessible way to learn about their roots while taking part in activities that reflect their lives today.Read full storyDID YOU KNOWNRI SPOTLIGHTLEMONCHILLINews that hits like a meme, but sticks like a fact.
